notes: Order differs slightly from B1-C1: here Jerusha hears the news first and then sees the trustee from behind, while in the original (and B1-C1) she sees the shadow on her way to the office. A reader would not stumble, but 'Before that, in the hall, she saw the man only from behind.' would align the levels.
Mrs. Lippett is named without introduction; 'One evening, Mrs. Lippett, the head of the home, called her.' would help absolute beginners.

'In the hall, she saw the trustee only from behind.' comes after the office conversation, so it reads as if she saw him afterwards; the original and B1-C1 place it before. Optional fix: 'Before that, in the hall, she saw the trustee only from behind.'
Grammar stays within present/past simple plus modals; vocabulary is suitable.
'As a boy, he spent his summers on this very farm.' would read more naturally as 'had spent', which B1 rules allow; optional.

No conditionals or passive found; plot (first Wednesday, headlight shadow, essay, John Smith, Lock Willow attic books, refused visit to Sallie's, scholarship, rejected first novel, proposal, New York reveal) matches the novel.
'He looked exactly like a daddy-long-legs' refers to the man rather than the shadow; 'It looked exactly like a daddy-long-legs' is slightly more precise. Taste only.

Details faithful to the original: surname from the telephone book, trustee had sent only boys before, secretary answering about money, flowers during her illness, scholarship, first earnings sent as repayment.
The quoted letter line ('the whole world seems to have read this book except me...') is invented, not from the novel; acceptable as a retelling but could be framed as paraphrase.
Quiz Q2 wording 'Why was Judy angry in her second summer at first?' is a little awkward; 'Why was Judy angry at the start of her second summer?' reads better.
Prose is genuinely literary without padding; the closing sentence tying the shadow, the reader of the letters and the man she loved is effective.

summary: All five levels are faithful to Jean Webster's novel in events, order and ending, with natural English, grammar appropriate to each level, correct quiz keys and nothing unsuitable for a 4+ audience. Only minor notes: A1/A2 place the shadow sighting after the news rather than before, and a few small wording preferences.
